teile.einleitung: The Glarus Thrust is a place where you can see especially clearly how the Alps were formed. There, old rocks lie on top of much younger ones, along a sharp line in the rock.
wichtigste: At the Glarus Thrust, older rocks lie on top of much younger ones.
On top lies reddish Verrucano from the Permian, below it Flysch from the early Tertiary.
The upper mass of rock was pushed about 40 kilometres northwards.
Since 2008 the area has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona.
Near Sool you can see the thrust surface up close at the Lochsite.
Twice a year the sun shines through the Martinsloch onto the church in Elm.

abschnitte.text: Normally younger layers of rock lie on top and older ones below. At the **Glarus Thrust** it is the other way round. On top lies the reddish **Verrucano**, a coarse rubble rock from the **Permian**, around 260 to 300 million years old. Below it lies **Flysch** from the **early Tertiary**, only about 35 to 50 million years old.

When the Alps were formed, the upper mass of rock was pushed about **40 kilometres** northwards over the younger layers. This is called a **thrust**. The boundary between the rocks is a sharp line that can be seen from far away in the mountain walls. At the **Lochsite** near **Sool** in the Sernf Valley you can even touch it.

The Zurich geologist **Albert Heim** first explained the layout with a **“double fold”**, that is, two folds lying against each other. The Frenchman **Marcel Bertrand** recognised a single great thrust as early as **1884**, without ever having been there. Heim only accepted this interpretation in **1902**. This gave rise to the **nappe theory**, which explains the structure of the Alps.

Since **2008** the area has belonged to the **UNESCO World Heritage** as the **Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona**. It lies in the cantons of Glarus, St Gallen and the Grisons. In the **Tschingelhörner** there is a natural hole in the rock, the **Martinsloch**. Twice a year the sun shines through it exactly onto the church of **Elm**.

gewusst: The thrust line is so clear that in good light you can see it from far away as a pale band in the rock walls.
The name Verrucano comes from a mountain in Tuscany in Italy, where a similar rock is found.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a small country, but it sells a great many goods and services abroad. This export economy is especially important for jobs and prosperity in the country.
wichtigste: Switzerland mainly exports pharmaceutical products, chemicals, machinery, watches and precision instruments.
The European Union is overall Switzerland’s most important trading partner.
As a single country, the USA was the biggest buyer of Swiss exports in 2024.
Switzerland has been a founding member of EFTA since 1960.
Since 2014 a free trade agreement has applied between Switzerland and China.
A strong franc makes Swiss products more expensive abroad.

abschnitte.text: The largest part of the exports is made up of **pharmaceutical products** and chemicals, such as medicines from Basel. In addition come machinery, watches and fine measuring instruments. **Gold** also plays a big role: a lot of gold is processed and traded in Switzerland. Because gold is very valuable, the export figures therefore fluctuate strongly from year to year.

The **European Union** is overall the most important trading partner, because Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe. With the EU, **bilateral agreements** regulate trade. If you look at single countries, in 2024 the **USA** came first, ahead of Germany. Countries such as China, Italy and France are important too.

In 1960 Switzerland was a founding member of **EFTA**, the European Free Trade Association. Through EFTA and also on its own it has concluded many **free trade agreements**. Such agreements lower or abolish customs duties. Since 1 July 2014 an agreement with **China** has applied, which made Switzerland one of the first countries in Europe to have one.

On 6 December 1992 the people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the **European Economic Area (EEA)**. After that Switzerland negotiated individual agreements with the EU, the so-called **bilateral path**. This path is still debated in politics today. It strongly shapes Switzerland’s foreign economic policy.

If the franc becomes stronger, customers abroad have to pay more for Swiss goods. This is called an **appreciation**. That is why in 2011 the **Swiss National Bank (SNB)** introduced a minimum rate of 1.20 francs per euro. In January 2015 it unexpectedly abolished it, and the franc suddenly became stronger. Many export firms had to save money or cut their prices.

gewusst: The organisation **Switzerland Global Enterprise** helps small and medium-sized firms take the step abroad, on behalf of the Confederation.
Because of the gold trade, Swiss export figures can be especially high in some years, although no gold is mined in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Grimsel Pass is an Alpine pass between the canton of Bern and the canton of Valais. It is known for its large reservoirs, which generate electricity, and for the source of the Aare.
wichtigste: The Grimsel Pass links the Bernese Oberland with Upper Valais.
The top of the pass is at around 2,164 metres above sea level.
On the Bernese side the road runs through the Haslital.
On the Valais side lies the small village of Gletsch.
Around the Grimsel there are several reservoirs that supply electricity.
The Aare rises at the Aare glaciers on the Grimsel.
The watershed between the Rhine and the Rhône runs over the top of the pass.

abschnitte.text: The Grimsel road begins at **Innertkirchen** in the Bernese Oberland. It climbs through the **Haslital**, where **Meiringen** also lies. The top of the pass is at around **2,164 metres**. On the Valais side it goes down to **Gletsch**. From there you can continue over the Furka Pass or into the Goms. In winter the pass road is closed because of snow.

On the Grimsel, several valleys were closed off with high **dams**. This created large artificial lakes. The largest is the **Lake Grimsel** near the top of the pass on the Bernese side. Right on the top of the pass, by contrast, lies a small natural lake, the **Totensee**. It lies right beside the road.

The water from the reservoirs flows through tunnels and pipes to **power stations**. There it drives **turbines** that generate electricity. The power stations on the Grimsel are among the important hydropower plants in Switzerland. A special attraction is the **Gelmerbahn**, a very steep funicular railway up to Lake Gelmer.

The **Aare** rises at the **Aare glaciers** near the Grimsel. It flows down through the Haslital into **Lake Brienz**. Later it flows through Bern and finally joins the Rhine. The Aare is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland.

A **watershed** runs over the top of the Grimsel Pass. This is a line where it is decided which way rainwater flows. To the north it flows via the Aare to the **Rhine** and into the **North Sea**. To the south it flows via the **Rhône** into the **Mediterranean**. So a raindrop on the top of the pass can end up in two quite different seas.

gewusst: The Rhône rises very close by, at the Rhône Glacier above Gletsch.
The Gelmerbahn is one of the steepest funicular railways in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The **Emmental** is a hilly landscape in the canton of Bern. It is known for large farmhouses, covered wooden bridges, cheese and Swiss wrestling. The name comes from the river Emme, which flows through the valley.
wichtigste: The Emmental is a landscape with many green hills in the canton of Bern.
Typical are scattered single farms with large, deep roofs.
Next to the farmhouse there is often a Stöckli for the older generation.
Covered wooden bridges lead over the Emme.
On its edge lies the Napf, in whose streams you can find tiny grains of gold.
Gotthelf’s story “The Black Spider” is set in the Emmental.

abschnitte.text: The Emmental is a landscape with **many green hills**, meadows and woods. The farms often lie singly on the slopes and on the hill ridges, which are called **Eggen**. These **scattered single farms** are typical, and there are fewer large closed villages. On the edge of the Emmental lies the **Napf**, a viewpoint mountain about 1,400 metres high on the border of the cantons of Bern and Lucerne.

The old **Emmental farmhouses** have huge roofs that reach almost to the ground. Under the roof there is room for the living quarters, the stable and the hay. Next to the big house there is often a smaller house, the **Stöckli**. When the young people take over the farm, the parents move into the Stöckli. In this way the generations stay close together.

In the Emmental a lot of milk is made into **cheese**. The cheesemakers warm the milk in large **copper vats** until it thickens. From it they shape large wheels of cheese. The best-known cheese is **Emmental** with its large holes. It carries the name of the valley out into the whole world.

Several old **covered wooden bridges** with a roof lead over the Emme. Very popular in the Emmental is Swiss wrestling, called **Schwingen**. In it two men or women wrestle in **linen shorts** on sawdust. In the streams on the Napf lie tiny **flakes of gold**. With luck and patience you can wash them out with a pan.

The pastor and writer **Jeremias Gotthelf** lived in **Lützelflüh** in the Emmental. Many of his stories tell of life on the farms. His eerie story **“Die schwarze Spinne”** (“The Black Spider”) appeared in 1842. It is set in the area of **Sumiswald** in the Emmental and is still read in schools today.

gewusst: With luck you can find real gold in the streams on the Napf, but only tiny grains.
The roofs of Emmental farmhouses sometimes reach almost to the ground.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background. It is one of the best-known symbols of Switzerland and has a special, square shape.
wichtigste: The Swiss flag is red and white.
It shows a white cross in the middle.
The flag is square, as otherwise only the flag of Vatican City is.
The sign of the Red Cross looks like the Swiss flag with the colours swapped.
On 1 August lanterns and bonfires light up everywhere.
Many Swiss products carry the Swiss cross.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Switzerland has a **red** background and a **white cross** in the middle. The four arms of the cross are equally long. The cross does not touch the edge. A similar sign was carried earlier by the canton of Schwyz, after which Switzerland is named.

Most flags in the world are rectangular. The Swiss flag, by contrast, is **square**. Only one other state also has a square flag: **Vatican City** in Rome. On ships, however, Switzerland uses a rectangular flag.

The **Red Cross** was founded in **Geneva** in 1863, among others by **Henry Dunant**. It helps injured and needy people. As its sign people chose the Swiss flag with **swapped colours**: a red cross on a white background. In this way they honoured Switzerland as the country of its founding.

On **1 August**, the national holiday, flags hang everywhere. In the evening **lanterns** and **bonfires** glow. Many Swiss products, such as pocket knives, watches or chocolate, show the **Swiss cross**. In this way you can tell that they come from Switzerland. There are clear rules for this indication of origin.

gewusst: Every municipality and every canton of Switzerland also has a coat of arms of its own.
Since 1889 the law has laid down what the Swiss coat of arms looks like.

teile.einleitung: An erratic boulder is a large block of stone that does not match the rock of its surroundings. In the ice age glaciers often carried it many kilometres and left it lying.
wichtigste: Erratic boulders consist of rock that does not otherwise occur in the area.
Ice-age glaciers brought them from the Alps to the Central Plateau and as far as the Jura.
They are also called “erratic blocks”, from the Latin errare, to wander.
From about one cubic metre upwards we speak of an erratic boulder rather than of glacial debris.
The Pierres du Niton in Geneva are the starting point of Swiss height measurement.
Louis Agassiz made it known that erratic boulders come from glaciers.

abschnitte.titel: A stone in the wrong place
abschnitte.text: If a large **granite block** lies on the **Central Plateau**, that is strange, because there is no granite in the ground there. Such blocks are called **erratic boulders** or **erratic blocks**. This comes from the Latin word **errare**, to wander, because they seem to have travelled. From a volume of about one **cubic metre** upwards we speak of an erratic boulder.

In the ice ages huge glaciers reached from the Alps far into the lowlands. They carried stones along on and in the ice. When the ice melted, the blocks stayed lying. Granite blocks from the Valais on the slope of the **Jura** show that the **Rhône Glacier** once reached as far as the Jura. If you compare the rock with rocks in the Alps, you can work out where it came from.

In the past nobody could explain how the blocks came to their places. The naturalist **Louis Agassiz**, a professor in Neuchâtel, put forward the idea of a great **ice age** from 1837. Erratic boulders and glacial polish were important proof for him. Today this explanation is generally accepted.

In the harbour of **Geneva** two erratic boulders stick out of the lake, the **Pierres du Niton**. On the larger one lies a survey mark, the **Repère Pierre du Niton**. From it the heights of the whole of Switzerland were determined. According to the national survey it lies at **373.6 metres above sea level**.

In the past many erratic boulders were broken up and used as **building stone** for walls, steps and fountains. Later people began to protect them. The **Pierre des Marmettes** near Monthey in the Valais is a huge granite block from the Mont Blanc area. The Swiss Society for Natural Sciences bought it in 1906 in order to save it.

gewusst: On the Pierre des Marmettes there even stood a little house.
Some erratic boulders on the Central Plateau come from areas more than 100 kilometres away.

teile.einleitung: GLAMOS stands for “Glacier Monitoring Switzerland”, the Swiss glacier measurement network. Every year it measures how Switzerland's glaciers are changing.
wichtigste: GLAMOS is run jointly by ETH Zurich, the University of Fribourg and the University of Zurich.
The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) is one of the funders.
Changes in the length of glaciers have been observed in Switzerland since 1880.
In 2024, the mass balance was measured directly in the field on around 20 glaciers.
One of the longest measurement series in the world has been running on the Clariden Firn since 1914/15.
A negative mass balance means that a glacier is shrinking.

abschnitte.text: **GLAMOS** is a joint programme of **ETH Zurich**, the **University of Fribourg** and the **University of Zurich**. It is supported, among others, by the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)**, MeteoSwiss and swisstopo. Switzerland has been observing its glaciers for a very long time: measurements of glacier lengths began in **1880**.

On almost **100 glaciers**, a measurement is taken every year of how far the **glacier snout** has moved. In 2023, 95 glaciers were surveyed, and almost all of them had retreated. This shows over many decades how the glaciers are changing.

The **mass balance** compares how much snow a glacier gains in winter with how much ice it loses in summer. If it is **negative**, the glacier loses more than it gains and shrinks. The calculation covers the **hydrological year** from 1 October to 30 September. In 2024 the mass balance was determined directly in the field on around **20 glaciers**.

Researchers drill **stakes** into the ice. When the ice melts, the stake sticks out further, and you can see how much has been lost. In snow pits they measure the amount of snow. With the **geodetic method**, they compare **elevation models** made from aerial photos or laser scans taken at two points in time. This shows how thickness and volume change.

On the **Clariden Firn** in the canton of Glarus, snow and ice have been measured at fixed points since **1914/15**. Together with the Silvretta Glacier, this series is one of the longest in the world. Such long series are valuable because they make it easy to see changes in the climate.

gewusst: Reports on the glaciers have appeared regularly in Switzerland since 1881.
The measurements in the field are extrapolated with models to all the glaciers in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The geography of Switzerland is very varied: in a small area there are high Alpine peaks, hills in the Central Plateau and the chains of the Jura. Each canton has its own highest point.
wichtigste: Switzerland consists of the Alps, the Central Plateau and the Jura.
The highest point of the canton of Uri is the Dammastock at 3,630 m.
At 3,614 m, the Tödi is the highest mountain in the canton of Glarus.
The Napf, at 1,408 m, is the highest point of the Central Plateau.
The Rheinwaldhorn is the highest mountain in Ticino.
Many of the cantons' highest points lie on cantonal borders.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland consists of three **major landscapes**: the **Alps** in the south, the **Central Plateau** in the middle and the **Jura** in the north-west. The Alps take up the largest part of the area. Most of the towns and cities are on the Central Plateau. The highest mountain in Switzerland is the **Dufourspitze** at 4,634 m in the Valais.

The highest point of the canton of **Uri** is the **Dammastock** at 3,630 m, on the border with the Valais. In **Glarus**, the **Tödi** rises to 3,614 m, the highest peak of the Glarus Alps. In the canton of **Schwyz** it is the **Bös Fulen** at around 2,802 m. In the canton of **Lucerne** it is the **Brienzer Rothorn** at 2,350 m, where Lucerne, Bern and Obwalden meet.

The **Napf**, between the Emmental and the Entlebuch, is the highest point of the **Central Plateau** at **1,408 m**. In the canton of **Fribourg**, the **Vanil Noir** at 2,389 m in the Gruyère region is the highest. In **Vaud**, the **Les Diablerets** massif at around 3,210 m forms the highest point, on the border with the Valais.

In the canton of **St Gallen**, the **Ringelspitz** at around 3,247 m is the highest peak, on the border with the Grisons. In **Ticino** it is the **Rheinwaldhorn**, also called the Adula, at 3,402 m on the border with the Grisons. It is striking that many highest points lie exactly on a **cantonal border**, because borders often run over peaks and ridges.

gewusst: The Napf is regarded as one of the finest viewpoints in the Central Plateau: in clear weather you can see the whole chain of the Alps.
In the mountains, cantonal borders often follow the watersheds, that is, the ridges between two valleys.

teile.einleitung: The **Emme** is a river in the canton of Bern. It rises in the Bernese Pre-Alps, flows north through the Emmental and joins the Aare near Solothurn. It is known for its dangerous floods.
wichtigste: The Emme rises on the Bolberg between the Hohgant and the Augstmatthorn.
It flows north through the Emmental.
The Emme is about 82 kilometres long.
Near Solothurn it flows into the Aare.
The town of Burgdorf with its castle lies on the Emme.
Emmental cheese is named after the valley of the Emme.

abschnitte.text: The Emme rises in the **canton of Bern** on the **Bolberg**, between the **Hohgant** and the **Augstmatthorn**. These mountains lie in the Bernese Pre-Alps north of **Lake Brienz**. From there the Emme first runs down the valley as a wild mountain stream. Then it reaches the hilly **Emmental**, which is named after it.

The Emme flows **north** through the Emmental. At the entrance to the Emmental lies the town of **Burgdorf**. Above its old town stands **Burgdorf Castle**. After about **82 kilometres** the Emme flows into the **Aare** near **Solothurn**, between Zuchwil and Luterbach. That makes it much shorter than the Aare.

In the past the Emme was especially feared for its dangerous **floods**. In a heavy thunderstorm the river can swell very quickly. Then it sweeps away stones, wood and sometimes bridges as well. The writer **Jeremias Gotthelf** described the great flood of **1837** in his story “Die Wassernot im Emmental” (“The Flood Disaster in the Emmental”). Today dams and river defences protect the villages better.

The famous **Emmental cheese** is named after the valley of the Emme, a cheese with large holes. Beware of confusion: in the **canton of Lucerne** there is a river of its own called the **Kleine Emme**, which means “Little Emme”. It has nothing to do with the Emme in the canton of Bern. The Kleine Emme flows into the Reuss at **Emmenbrücke**.

gewusst: Jeremias Gotthelf wrote a whole story about the flood of 1837, “Die Wassernot im Emmental”.
There are two Emmes: the Emme in the canton of Bern and the Kleine Emme in the canton of Lucerne.

teile.einleitung: A glacial lake outburst flood is the sudden bursting of a glacial lake, with a flood wave. In Switzerland, such events have repeatedly threatened valleys.
wichtigste: A glacial lake outburst flood is the sudden bursting of a lake dammed by ice or moraine.
In 1818 a lake outburst at the Giétro Glacier devastated the Val de Bagnes.
An ice dam can float once the lake is deep enough.
Moraine dams are dangerous because the loose debris erodes quickly.
An ice or rock fall into the lake can also trigger a flood wave.
Protective structures have been built at the Glacier de la Plaine Morte and in Grindelwald.

abschnitte.titel: What is a glacial lake outburst flood?
abschnitte.text: Sometimes glacier ice or a **moraine**, a wall of debris, dams a lake. If this dam suddenly breaks, a **flood wave** pours into the valley. This is called a **glacial lake outburst flood**. In Icelandic it is called a jökulhlaup, and in English people speak of a GLOF.

**Ice** is lighter than water. If a lake dammed by ice becomes deep enough, the water pressure lifts the ice dam: it begins to **float**, and the water drains away beneath the glacier. **Moraine dams** consist of loose debris and can **erode** quickly. If ice or rock falls into the lake, a surge wave is created that can flow over the dam.

Ice collapses from the **Giétro Glacier** dammed the Dranse in the Valais **Val de Bagnes** into a lake. The engineer **Ignaz Venetz** had a **tunnel** dug through the ice dam to lower the lake. This reduced the amount of water. In June 1818 the dam broke anyway, and the flood devastated the valley as far as Martigny.

At the **Glacier de la Plaine Morte**, the **Lac des Faverges** empties almost every year and threatens the **Simmental** near Lenk. In 2019 a **channel** about 800 m long was cut into the ice so that the water drains away continuously. At the **Lower Grindelwald Glacier**, a **relief tunnel** was built in 2009 so that the glacial lake could be emptied in a controlled way.

In June 2024, the glacial lake **Calderas** in the Grisons suddenly drained. The water triggered debris flows and hit the **Alp Flix** in the municipality of Surses. Because glaciers are melting, new lakes are forming in the Alps. Experts therefore watch them closely.

gewusst: Ignaz Venetz later also became known as one of the pioneers of the ice age theory.
When the Lac des Faverges bursts each year, the water flows via the Trüebbach into the Simme.

teile.einleitung: Bern is the seat of the government and Parliament of Switzerland. Even so, Bern is officially not called the capital but the **Bundesstadt** (federal city). Here you can find out why that is and what makes Bern the federal city.
wichtigste: The Federal Constitution does not set a capital of Switzerland.
Bern is the seat of the Federal Council, Parliament and the federal administration and is therefore called the federal city.
Before 1848 the leadership of the Diet changed every two years between Zurich, Bern and Lucerne.
At the end of 2023 Bern was only the fifth largest city in Switzerland.
After Zurich main station, Bern station is the station with the most passengers.
SBB and Swiss Post have their headquarters in the Wankdorf district of Bern.

abschnitte.text: In the **Federal Constitution** there is not a word about a capital. Switzerland is a federal state in which the cantons carry a lot of weight, and no city was meant to stand above the others. But Bern is the place where the **Federal Council**, **Parliament** and large parts of the **federal administration** work. That is why Bern is called the **federal city**. In everyday life, however, many people still say capital.

Before 1848 Switzerland was a confederation of states. The representatives of the cantons met at the **Diet** (Tagsatzung). After the **Federal Treaty of 1815** the leadership, the so-called **Vorort** (lead canton), changed every two years between Zurich, Bern and Lucerne. Only the new **federal state of 1848** needed a permanent seat for government and Parliament. The choice then fell on Bern.

Bern is not the largest city in the country. At the end of 2023 Bern was in fifth place behind **Zurich**, **Geneva**, **Basel** and **Lausanne**. Famous is the **old town** with its **arcades**. These covered walkways stretch for around six kilometres through the lanes. They are regarded as one of the longest covered shopping promenades in Europe, and the old town belongs to the UNESCO World Heritage.

Many federal offices lie not only in the city of Bern but also in municipalities around it, the **agglomeration**. For example, the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH) has its seat in the Liebefeld district of the municipality of **Köniz**. Companies close to the Confederation are also in Bern: the **SBB** and **Swiss Post** have their headquarters in the well-connected district of **Wankdorf**.

**Bern station** is the second largest station in Switzerland. Here important long-distance lines between east, west and south cross. Since 2010 there has been the association **Hauptstadtregion Schweiz** (Capital Region Switzerland). In it cantons, cities and regions work together. The **Swiss Spatial Concept** names this region alongside the three large metropolitan areas of Zurich, Basel and Geneva-Lausanne.

gewusst: Because the constitution knows no capital, Bern is legally speaking simply the “federal city”.
The arcades of Bern are together around six kilometres long, so in rain you can stroll through the old town almost dry.

teile.einleitung: The Gorner Glacier lies in the Monte Rosa massif south-east of Zermatt. Together with its side glaciers it forms one of the largest glacier areas in the Alps.
wichtigste: The Gorner Glacier lies in the Monte Rosa massif near Zermatt.
In 2017 the Gorner Glacier system was the second largest continuous glacier area in the Alps.
In 2013 the Gorner Glacier was around 12 km long.
The Grenz Glacier is the main arm and begins at the Signalkuppe.
It reached its last peak in 1859.
In 2019 the Gorner and Grenz glaciers separated.

abschnitte.text: The **Gorner Glacier** lies in the **Monte Rosa massif** south-east of **Zermatt**. At around 41 km², the **Gorner Glacier system** was the **second largest** continuous glacier area in the Alps in 2017, after the Aletsch Glacier. In 2013 the glacier was around **12 km** long. Its accumulation area reaches up to the summit region above 4,000 m.

The main arm of the system is the **Grenz Glacier**. It begins at the **Signalkuppe**, which is 4,554 m high, and flows north-west along the Lyskamm. On a rocky ridge above the former confluence, at 2,883 m, stands the **Monte Rosa Hut**. It is the starting point for tours up Monte Rosa.

Every spring the **Gornersee** forms where the Grenz and Gorner glaciers meet, held back by the ice. In summer it usually **drains** within a few days. The meltwater reaches Zermatt through streams and forms the **Matter Vispa** there, which flows through the Mattertal to the Rhône.

Until **1859** the glacier advanced and destroyed alpine huts and meadows. Since then it has been retreating. In 1850 the system covered about 66 km², and in 2015 only around 41 km². That is a decline of around **38 per cent**. In **2019** the link between the Gorner and Grenz glaciers even broke off.

gewusst: When the Gornersee bursts out, the flow in the Gornerbach can rise to as much as 150 cubic metres per second.
From the Gornergrat above Zermatt you have a wide view of the glacier and Monte Rosa.

teile.einleitung: The **European Continental Divide** is a long boundary line right across Europe. On one side of it water flows to the Atlantic, the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, on the other to the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. It also runs right across the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: The main watershed separates the Atlantic, the North Sea and the Baltic Sea from the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.
From the west it enters the Swiss Alps at Mont Pèlerin above Vevey.
The Lukmanier Pass separates the Rhine and the Po, the Albula Pass the Rhine and the Danube.
The Oberalp Pass and the Maloja Pass do not lie on the main watershed.
At the Witenwasserenstock the Rhine, Rhône and Po meet, as do Uri, the Valais and Ticino.
In the 17th century the Canal d’Entreroches was meant to overcome the watershed at the Mormont.

abschnitte.text: A **watershed** separates areas whose water flows in different directions. The **European Continental Divide** is the most important of them. On one side the water flows to the open **Atlantic**, the **North Sea** and the **Baltic Sea**. On the other side it flows to the **Mediterranean** and the **Black Sea**. From the west it enters the Swiss Alps at **Mont Pèlerin** above Vevey and then runs eastwards along the ridges of the Bernese Alps.

Several Alpine passes lie exactly on the main watershed. At the **Lukmanier Pass** the water flows north via the Medelser Rhine to the Rhine, and south through the Blenio Valley to the Ticino and to the **Po**. At the **Albula Pass** the Albula flows via the Hinterrhein to the **Rhine**. On the Engadine side the water flows into the Inn and on to the **Danube**. Both passes thus separate the area of the North Sea from that of the Mediterranean or Black Sea.

Not every watershed is also the main watershed. At the **Oberalp Pass** the water flows on one side into the Vorderrhein, on the other into the Reuss. Both belong to the Rhine area. At the **Maloja Pass** the water flows on one side via the Inn and the Danube into the Black Sea, on the other via the Mera to the Po and into the Adriatic. Both sides lie on the same side of the main watershed.

At the **Witenwasserenstock** there is a special point at 3,025 m above sea level. Here the catchment areas of the **Rhine**, **Rhône** and **Po** meet. At the same time the three cantons of **Uri**, **Valais** and **Ticino** meet here. The point lies about 224 metres east-south-east of the summit.

In the west of Switzerland the main watershed runs very low at the hill of **Mormont** in the canton of Vaud. That is why from **1638** people tried to build the **Canal d’Entreroches** here. It was meant to link **Lake Neuchâtel** with **Lake Geneva**. The canal ran from Yverdon through a cutting in the Mormont as far as the Venoge near Cossonay. The section to Lake Geneva was never built, because it would have needed about 40 more locks and the money ran out.

gewusst: At the Witenwasserenstock a raindrop can flow towards the North Sea, the Mediterranean or the Adriatic, depending on where it lands.
As early as the 17th century people wanted to travel by boat from Lake Neuchâtel to Lake Geneva on the Canal d’Entreroches.

teile.einleitung: On many mountain summits in Switzerland there stands a large cross, the summit cross. It shows that you have reached the highest point.
wichtigste: A summit cross marks the highest point of a mountain.
Many summit crosses are made of wood or metal.
The cross is a symbol from Christianity.
Often a summit book lies by the cross for people to write in.
Many walkers take a summit photo there.
In a thunderstorm a summit cross is dangerous, because lightning can strike it.

abschnitte.text: The **cross** is a symbol of **Christianity**. Centuries ago, people already put up crosses on mountains as a sign of faith and thanks. Today **summit crosses** mainly mark the **highest point** of a mountain. Not every summit has one: some mountains have a cairn instead, a tower of stones.

Many summit crosses are made of **wood** or **metal**. They often have to be carried up laboriously or brought by helicopter. Clubs, mountain guides or village communities often put up a cross and look after it. Wind, snow and sun are hard on the crosses.

By the cross there is often a **summit book** in a box. Climbers and walkers write their name and the date in it. Many take a **summit photo** and enjoy the view. Among mountaineers, people at the top often greet each other with **“Berg Heil”**.

A summit cross is the highest point for miles around, and often made of metal. In a **thunderstorm**, **lightning** can strike there. So if there is a risk of storms, you should avoid summits and ridges and come down in good time. It is important to check the weather forecast before a trip.

gewusst: Some old summit books are later kept in museums or archives.
Summit crosses are sometimes debated: some people see a religious symbol, others simply a summit marker.

teile.einleitung: Chur is the main town of the canton of Graubünden. The city lies in the Graubünden Rhine Valley and is often described as the **oldest city in Switzerland**. The Romans already had a base here.
wichtigste: Chur is the main town and largest city of the canton of Graubünden.
Chur lies on the Rhine, and the Plessur flows through the middle of the city.
Chur is often described as the oldest city in Switzerland.
The Romans called the place Curia.
The diocese of Chur is regarded as the oldest diocese north of the Alps.
The Arosa Railway runs through the streets of Chur like a tram.

abschnitte.text: Chur is the largest city and the **main town** of the canton of **Graubünden**. Here the cantonal government and the **Grand Council**, the canton's parliament, work. The city lies in the **Graubünden Rhine Valley**. From there the **Rhine** flows on towards Lake Constance. Right through Chur flows the **Plessur**, which comes from the Schanfigg and flows into the Rhine on the edge of the city.

In the area of Chur people lived over 10,000 years ago. That is why Chur is often described as the **oldest city in Switzerland**. The **Romans** had a base here called **Curia**. From this name Chur later came. The position was favourable, because from here routes led to several Alpine passes.

For many centuries a **bishop** has had his seat in Chur. The **diocese of Chur** is regarded as the oldest diocese north of the Alps. The bishop lives in the **Hof district** above the old town. There also stands the large bishop's church, the **Cathedral of the Assumption of Mary**. It was built in the 12th and 13th centuries.

Chur is an important railway junction of the **Rhaetian Railway**. The **Arosa Railway** starts at the station and at first rolls like a tram right through the streets of the city. Then it runs up to Arosa. Straight from the old town a **cable car** takes visitors up the local mountain **Brambrüesch**. There you can walk and, in winter, ski.

gewusst: From the Roman name Curia the present name Chur came about.
In Chur a train of the Arosa Railway runs right through the streets, just like a tram.

teile.einleitung: Zurich is the most important centre for banks, insurance companies and stock market trading in Switzerland. That is why people speak of Zurich as a financial centre.
wichtigste: The Paradeplatz is regarded as a symbol of the Swiss banking centre.
The Swiss stock exchange SIX Swiss Exchange has its seat in Zurich.
The SMI (Swiss Market Index) covers the 20 largest firms on the stock exchange.
In 2023 UBS took over Credit Suisse.
The Swiss National Bank has seats in Bern and Zurich.
Banks and insurance companies belong to the tertiary sector, the services.

abschnitte.text: On the **Paradeplatz** in the middle of Zurich stand the head offices of large banks. It is therefore regarded as a symbol of the Swiss **banking centre**. Banks keep money safe, grant loans and manage assets. So they offer **services** and belong to the **tertiary sector**.

On a stock exchange, shares and other securities are traded. The most important stock exchange in Switzerland is the **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich. The best-known stock index is called the **SMI**, Swiss Market Index. It covers the **20** largest and most heavily traded firms. If the SMI rises, these shares are worth more on average.

Large insurance companies also have their seats in Zurich. A special kind is **reinsurance**: it insures other insurance companies. In this way an insurance company can also pay very large losses, for example after a storm or earthquake. One of the largest reinsurers in the world has its seat in Zurich.

abschnitte.titel: National Bank and changes in banking
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank (SNB)** has its seat in **Bern and Zurich**. It makes sure the franc stays stable. In March 2023 the bank **Credit Suisse** got into great difficulties. With the help of the Confederation and the SNB, **UBS** took it over so that the financial system stayed stable.

For a long time Switzerland was known for **banking secrecy**. Banks had to keep information about their customers secret. Other countries criticised that taxes could be evaded in this way. Today Switzerland automatically exchanges information about accounts with many countries.

gewusst: The SIX Swiss Exchange runs not only the stock exchange but also systems for payments in Switzerland.
Switzerland is one of the most important places in the world for managing assets from abroad.

t1g6h434.t: Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments of National Importance

teile.einleitung: The BLN is the Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments of National Importance. It is a list of the most valuable landscapes in Switzerland. The Confederation must treat these areas with special care in carrying out its tasks.
wichtigste: The BLN covers 162 objects.
Together they cover around 19 per cent of the country's area.
The BLN is based on the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage (NHG) of 1966.
The first objects were included in 1977, the last in 1998.
It is binding on federal bodies when they carry out federal tasks.
In 2017 the BLN was revised with precise protection aims.

abschnitte.text: The **BLN** is a list of **162 objects**. It includes large mountain landscapes, lakeshores, bogs and gorges, but also small **natural monuments**. A typical natural monument is an **erratic boulder**, that is, a large stone that a glacier carried a long way. Rock outcrops and other **geotopes** belong to it too. Together the objects cover around **19 per cent** of the country's area.

The BLN is based on Article 5 of the **Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage (NHG)**. This act came into force on 1 July **1966**. The first series of BLN objects was determined in **1977**. By **1998** three more series followed. The basis was the private **KLN inventory**, which was drawn up from 1959 to 1963 by Pro Natura, the Heimatschutz (Swiss Heritage Society) and the SAC (Swiss Alpine Club).

The BLN is directly binding on **federal bodies carrying out federal tasks**. This concerns, for example, permits, concessions or subsidies from the Confederation. According to Article 6 NHG, BLN objects should be **preserved intact** or at least spared as much as possible. Exceptions are only possible if there are equal or higher interests of national importance. The BLN has no direct legal effect on property ownership.

In **2017** the Federal Council approved a **revision** of the BLN. Since then every object has a precise description and concrete **protection aims**. This makes it clearer what is especially valuable about a landscape. Some names were also adjusted. Besides the BLN there are further federal inventories, such as the **ISOS** for townscapes and the **IVS** for historic transport routes.

gewusst: BLN objects include well-known landscapes such as the Rhine Falls or the region around the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
Almost a fifth of Switzerland is thus recorded as especially valuable landscape.

teile.einleitung: Farmers in Switzerland receive money from the Confederation, so-called **direct payments**. They compensate for services from which everyone benefits: well-kept landscapes, biodiversity and animal welfare. Here you can find out how the system works.
wichtigste: Every year the Confederation pays around 2.8 billion francs in direct payments.
The basis is Article 104 of the Federal Constitution of 1996.
A precondition is the proof of ecological performance (PEP).
As a rule, 7 per cent of the area must be biodiversity promotion areas.
The Federal Office for Agriculture is responsible, and payment is made through the cantons.
There are, for example, RAUS contributions, slope contributions and landscape quality contributions.

abschnitte.text: In the past the state guaranteed farmers fixed **prices** and the **purchase** of their products. That led to **overproduction**, for example to mountains of butter and cheese. Today the Confederation instead pays **direct payments**. They compensate for **services in the public interest**, that is, work done for the community, and do not depend on the quantity produced. These include landscape care and biodiversity.

The basis is **Article 104** of the **Federal Constitution**. The people accepted it in **1996**. It describes the tasks of agriculture, such as the secure supply of food and the care of the cultural landscape. The **Federal Office for Agriculture** (FOAG) is responsible for putting it into practice. The money is paid out through the **cantons**. For years the total has been around **2.8 billion francs** a year.

Direct payments are only given if a farm provides the **proof of ecological performance**, **PEP** for short. This includes a balanced **fertiliser budget**, so no more fertiliser than necessary. A regulated **crop rotation** is also important, so that the same thing does not grow in a field every year. As a rule, **7 per cent** of the agricultural area must be **biodiversity promotion areas**, such as extensive meadows or hedges.

Part of the direct payments promotes **animal welfare**. Farms whose animals are regularly allowed outdoors receive the **RAUS contributions**. RAUS stands for “regelmässiger Auslauf ins Freie”, which means regular access to the outdoors. The animals then go on the pasture or into an outdoor run. In this way the Confederation supports animal-friendly husbandry.

Steep meadows are hard to mow and need a lot of work. That is why mountain farmers receive **slope contributions**. They belong to the **cultural landscape contributions** and are meant to prevent such areas from **becoming overgrown**, that is, growing over with scrub. With agricultural policy 2014 to 2017 the **landscape quality contributions** were added. In regional projects of the cantons they promote, for example, standard fruit orchards or dry-stone walls.

gewusst: RAUS is an abbreviation and means “regelmässiger Auslauf ins Freie”, regular access to the outdoors.
Direct payments are the largest part of the Confederation’s spending on agriculture.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Pass is one of the most famous Alpine passes in Switzerland. It links the canton of Uri in the north with the canton of Ticino in the south and was already an important route across the Alps in the Middle Ages.
wichtigste: The Gotthard Pass links Uri with Ticino.
The top of the pass is at around 2,100 metres above sea level.
Andermatt lies on the north side and Airolo on the south side.
The Tremola is a winding, cobbled road on the Ticino side.
The Devil's Bridge crosses the Reuss in the Schöllenen Gorge.
The first railway tunnel opened in 1882 and the road tunnel in 1980.
In winter the pass road is closed because of snow.

abschnitte.titel: A pass between north and south
abschnitte.text: A **pass** is a crossing over a mountain at the lowest possible point. The Gotthard lies in the middle of the Swiss Alps. From **Andermatt** in the canton of Uri, the road climbs to the top of the pass at just over 2,100 metres. On the other side it goes down to **Airolo** in Ticino. At the top of the pass there are small lakes, a museum and the old hospice.

The way from the north to the Gotthard leads through the narrow **Schöllenen Gorge**. There the **Reuss** roars between steep rock walls. For a long time this gorge was almost impossible to cross. In the Middle Ages only a bridge made the route possible: the **Devil's Bridge**. A well-known legend says that the devil built it and demanded as his reward the first soul to cross the bridge.

On the Ticino side, the **Tremola** winds down from the top of the pass towards Airolo. It has very many tight bends and is **cobbled** with stones. Today most cars use a newer road beside it. But the Tremola is popular with cyclists and day-trippers because it is so impressive.

Since the Middle Ages there has been a **hospice** at the top of the pass. This is a building where travellers could stay the night and warm up. In the past, **muleteers** carried goods over the pass with mules. In winter there is a great deal of snow at the top and there is a danger of **avalanches**. That is why the pass road is closed for several months every year.

Today most people travel under the Gotthard. The first **railway tunnel** between Göschenen and Airolo opened in **1882** and was then the longest tunnel in the world. Since **1980** there has been the **Gotthard Road Tunnel** for cars. In 2016 the much longer **Gotthard Base Tunnel** was added, which lies deeper in the mountain.

gewusst: At the Gotthard the paths of the water part: the Reuss flows north to the Rhine, the Ticino south to the Po.
At around 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is one of the longest railway tunnels in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is a railway tunnel deep beneath the Gotthard massif. At 57 kilometres it is the longest railway tunnel in the world (as of 2025).
wichtigste: Trains run through the Gotthard Base Tunnel.
At 57 km it is the longest railway tunnel in the world (as of 2025).
In the north it begins at Erstfeld in the canton of Uri.
It has two tubes for the trains.
Building it cost around 12 billion francs.
It opened in 2016 and shortens the journey to Ticino.

abschnitte.text: The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** is around **57 km** long, which makes it the **longest railway tunnel in the world** (as of 2025). It overtook the **Seikan Tunnel** in Japan. It opened in **2016**. It begins in the north at **Erstfeld** in the canton of Uri and ends in the south at Bodio in Ticino.

A **base tunnel** lies deep down at the **foot of the mountain**, not high up like older tunnels. This means the trains hardly have to climb. The highest point in the tunnel is only around **549 m above sea level**. So long, heavy freight trains can run fast, and travellers reach **Ticino** sooner.

The tunnel has **two tubes**, one for each direction. They are connected at regular intervals by cross passages. In an emergency, people can escape into the other tube. About a third and two thirds of the way along are the **multifunction stations at Sedrun and Faido**, with emergency stops.

The building work took many years and cost around **12 billion francs**. Tunnel boring machines ate their way through the hard rock. The tunnel is part of **NEAT**, the New Rail Link through the Alps. It is meant to move more goods from the road onto the **railway** and so protect the Alps.

gewusst: Inside the mountain, the rock can be over 40 °C, so the tunnel needs cooling.
Government representatives from several neighbouring countries attended the opening in 2016.

teile.einleitung: Gruyère, in German Greyerzer, is one of the best-known cheeses in Switzerland. It is named after the Gruyère region in the canton of Fribourg and is made from raw cow's milk.
wichtigste: Gruyère is made from raw cow's milk.
In German it is called “Greyerzer”.
It is a hard cheese and has almost no holes.
It matures for at least about five months in the cellar.
A wheel usually weighs between 25 and 40 kilograms.
Gruyère is an important ingredient in cheese fondue.

abschnitte.text: **Gruyère** takes its name from the region of **Gruyères** (in German Greyerz) in the canton of **Fribourg**. The pretty little town of Gruyères with its castle is also there. Today the cheese is also made in neighbouring cantons. Its name is protected as **AOP**. That means only cheese from a certain area and made according to fixed rules may carry the name.

A **cheesemaker** turns milk into cheese in the **dairy**. For Gruyère you need **raw cow's milk** from cows in the region. The milk is warmed in a big copper vat and curdled. Then the mass is broken up, put into moulds and pressed. This produces a round, flat **wheel**, which usually weighs between 25 and 40 kilograms.

Fresh cheese is still soft. So the wheels go into a **cool, damp cellar**. There they are regularly **turned** and rubbed with **salt water**. This forms a firm rind. A Gruyère matures for at least about **five months**. Many wheels mature for even longer and then taste stronger and more savoury.

Gruyère is a **hard cheese**. Its body is firm and even, and it has **almost no holes**. In this it differs from Emmental with its large holes. Young Gruyère tastes mild, while old Gruyère is savoury and sometimes slightly grainy.

Gruyère **melts well**. That is why it is in many recipes for **cheese fondue**. In the well-known “moitié-moitié” fondue, it is mixed with Vacherin Fribourgeois. It is also eaten with bread, in cheese tart or grated over a gratin. Gruyère is sold to many countries of the world.

gewusst: In Pringy near Gruyères there is a show dairy where you can watch cheese being made.
A single wheel of Gruyère needs several hundred litres of milk.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland people are on average getting older and older. At the same time fewer children are being born. This interplay is called **demographic ageing**. It changes the world of work, pension provision and healthcare.
wichtigste: Life expectancy in Switzerland is among the highest in the world.
In 2024 it was around 86 years at birth for women and 82.5 years for men.
Around one fifth of the population is aged 65 or older.
The baby boomers, born roughly between 1946 and 1964, are now reaching retirement age.
The old-age dependency ratio compares the over 64s with the 20 to 64 year olds.
The population pyramid of Switzerland has the shape of an urn.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **demographic ageing** when the share of older people in the population grows. Two reasons are important: people live longer, and fewer children are born. **Demography** is the science that studies the population and its development. In Switzerland the **Federal Statistical Office** (FSO) collects the figures.

**Life expectancy** states how old people become on average. According to the FSO, in **2024** it was around **86 years** at birth for women and **82.5 years** for men. This puts Switzerland among the best in the world. Reasons include good nutrition, safe jobs and good medical care.

After the **Second World War** birth numbers rose strongly. The people born in the years from about **1946 to 1964** are called **baby boomers**. These large birth cohorts are now gradually reaching **retirement age**. In 2023 around **one fifth** of the population, that is about 19 to 20 per cent, were aged 65 or older. This share is still rising.

The **old-age dependency ratio** shows how many people aged 65 and over there are for every 100 people of working age, 20 to 64. If it rises, fewer people in work have to provide for more pensioners. In the past the **population pyramid** really did look like a pyramid, with many young people at the bottom. Today the base is narrow and the middle broad. This shape is called the **urn shape**.

Ageing has consequences for **pension provision**. The **AHV**, the state old-age and survivors’ insurance, is financed mainly by those who are in work today. When there are more pensioners, it needs more money. More staff are also needed in **healthcare** and in care for the elderly. How to solve these tasks is a political debate, for example about the retirement age or the financing of the AHV.

gewusst: In Switzerland women live several years longer than men on average.
The population pyramid of Switzerland is today really no longer a pyramid at all but looks more like an urn.

teile.einleitung: French is one of the four national languages of Switzerland. It is spoken mainly in the west, in the Romandie, and has some words of its own there.
wichtigste: French is the second largest national language of Switzerland.
The French-speaking part of Switzerland is called the Romandie, its inhabitants Romands.
In the Romandie people say septante for 70 and nonante for 90.
In Vaud people say huitante for 80.
Many Romands call lunch dîner and the evening meal souper.
Lake Geneva is mostly called Lac Léman in French.

abschnitte.text: After German, French is the **second largest national language** of Switzerland. It is spoken in the **Romandie** in the west. Entirely French-speaking are the cantons of **Geneva**, **Vaud**, **Neuchâtel** and **Jura**. In **Fribourg**, in the **Valais** and in **Bern** people speak German and French.

In France people say “soixante-dix” for 70, that is, sixty plus ten. In the Romandie people say more simply **septante**. For 90 they say **nonante** instead of “quatre-vingt-dix”. In **Vaud**, in Fribourg and in the Valais people often say **huitante** for 80. In Belgium too people say septante and nonante.

There are differences with meals too. Many Romands call breakfast **déjeuner**, lunch **dîner** and the evening meal **souper**. In France, by contrast, lunch is mostly called “déjeuner” and the evening meal “dîner”. On visits this can lead to funny misunderstandings.

**Lake Geneva** is mostly called **Lac Léman** in French. Some words in the Romandie come from German, for example “poutzer” for putzen, to clean. Such special features are called **Helvetisms**. They show how the languages in Switzerland influence one another.

gewusst: In the past various dialects were spoken in the Romandie, called Franco-Provençal, which has almost disappeared today.
In Biel/Bienne German and French have equal status, and the street signs are bilingual.

teile.einleitung: In Bellinzona, the main town of the canton of Ticino, stand three mighty castles. Together with long walls they used to block the valley. Today they belong to the **UNESCO World Heritage** and are a popular destination for outings.
wichtigste: In Bellinzona stand three castles: Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro.
Castelgrande is the largest castle and stands on a rocky hill in the middle of the city.
Sasso Corbaro lies highest, Montebello lies in between.
The castles and walls blocked the way through the valley to the Alpine passes.
The Dukes of Milan had the castles greatly extended.
Since the year 2000 the castles have belonged to the UNESCO World Heritage.

abschnitte.titel: Three castles one above the other
abschnitte.text: The three castles lie as if on a staircase. Below in the city stands **Castelgrande**, which means “big castle”. Higher up the slope lies **Montebello**, the middle castle. Right at the top **Sasso Corbaro** stands enthroned. From there you can see far out into the valley.

Bellinzona lies at a narrow spot in the Ticino valley. Here routes meet that lead to important **Alpine passes** such as the Gotthard, Lukmanier and San Bernardino. With castles and walls this route could be blocked. From Castelgrande a long wall, the **Murata**, runs right across the valley to the river **Ticino**. Anyone who wanted to go through the valley had to get past this barrier.

In the Middle Ages Bellinzona long belonged to the Duchy of **Milan**. The **Dukes of Milan** greatly extended the castles to protect themselves against the Confederates in the north. Around 1500 Bellinzona nevertheless came under the rule of the Confederates from Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden. After that the castles were no longer needed for wars.

abschnitte.titel: World Heritage and destination for outings
abschnitte.text: Since the year **2000** the three castles and the city walls have belonged to the **UNESCO World Heritage**. They are regarded as an especially well-preserved example of a medieval fortification. Today you can visit the castles. An easy way is a **lift** that runs up inside the rock of Castelgrande from the old town.

gewusst: The name Castelgrande simply means “big castle” in Italian.
The lift to Castelgrande runs up right through the rock.

teile.einleitung: The **Entlebuch** is a rural mountain region in the canton of Lucerne. It lies between the city of Lucerne and the Emmental. The region is known for its bogs and landscapes, which are protected as the **Entlebuch Biosphere**.
wichtigste: The Entlebuch lies in the canton of Lucerne and covers about 400 km².
The Glaubenberg Pass links the Entlebuch with Sarnen.
Sörenberg lies at the foot of the Brienzer Rothorn.
The Biosphere Centre is in Schüpfheim.
About a third of the workforce works in agriculture and forestry.
The Entlebucher Mountain Dog is the smallest Swiss mountain dog breed.

abschnitte.text: The Entlebuch lies in the **canton of Lucerne**, between the city of Lucerne and the **Emmental**. The region covers an area of **397 km²**. That is clearly more than the whole canton of Zug. Part of the border with the Bernese Emmental is formed by the river **Ilfis**. This border was already fixed in the 15th century.

The **Glaubenberg Pass** at 1,543 m above sea level links the Entlebuch with **Sarnen** in the canton of Obwalden. In the upper Entlebuch lies the holiday resort of **Sörenberg**. It belongs to the municipality of **Flühli** and lies at the foot of the **Brienzer Rothorn**. A cable car runs up to the summit. In winter Sörenberg is a popular ski area.

The Entlebuch is a **UNESCO biosphere reserve**. In a biosphere reserve nature is to be protected, and at the same time the people there are to be able to live and work well. Especially valuable are the many **bogs** of the region. The **Biosphere Centre** is in **Schüpfheim**. From there the biosphere reserve is looked after.

In the Entlebuch many people work in **agriculture and forestry**, about a third of the workforce. In the Swiss average it is only a few per cent. The **Entlebucher Mountain Dog** also comes from the region. It is the smallest of the four Swiss mountain dog breeds. In the past it helped the farmers to drive their cattle.

gewusst: An “Entlebucher” can also be a dog: the Entlebucher Mountain Dog.
The Entlebuch is larger than the whole canton of Zug.

teile.einleitung: Campione d'Italia is a small place on Lake Lugano that belongs to Italy but is entirely surrounded by Switzerland. Such an area is called an **exclave**. For a long time life there was almost like in Switzerland, today it is more closely tied to Italy.
wichtigste: Campione d'Italia lies on the eastern shore of Lake Lugano.
On land the place is completely enclosed by the canton of Ticino.
The municipality belongs to the Italian province of Como in Lombardy.
Since 1 January 2020 Campione has belonged to the customs territory of the EU.
Until the end of 2019 the cars had Ticino number plates.
The official currency is the euro, whereas in the past people mostly paid in francs.
The casino is well known, and its new building was designed by Mario Botta.

abschnitte.text: Campione d'Italia lies on the **eastern shore of Lake Lugano**. On one side is the lake, and on the land side the place borders only municipalities of the **canton of Ticino**. Anyone who wants to travel from Campione to Italy has to use Swiss roads. Politically, Campione is a municipality of the **province of Como** in the region of **Lombardy**.

In the Middle Ages a man called **Toto of Campione** left the place in the year 777 to the **monastery of Sant'Ambrogio** in Milan. The monastery owned Campione until 1797. That is why the place did not come to the Confederation like the rest of Ticino. In **1933** the Fascist dictator **Benito Mussolini** had the addition “d'Italia” attached to the name. In this way he wanted to stress that the place belongs to Italy.

For a long time everyday life in Campione was closely tied to Switzerland. Until the end of 2019 the place in fact belonged to the **Swiss customs territory**. The cars ran with **Ticino number plates** (TI), and in everyday life people mostly paid in **Swiss francs**. Most landline connections still have the Swiss dialling code **+41** today. People who ring from Italy therefore dial 0041.

abschnitte.titel: In the EU customs territory since 2020
abschnitte.text: Since **1 January 2020** Campione has belonged to the **customs territory of the European Union**. Since then cars have had to be registered in Italy. Officially the **euro** applies, because Campione is a part of Italy. The place is known for its **casino**. The large new building was designed by the Ticino architect **Mario Botta**, and it opened in 2007.

gewusst: Anyone who telephones Campione d'Italia from Italy mostly rings with the Swiss dialling code 0041.
When it opened in 2007 the casino of Campione was one of the largest casinos in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The **Valais** is the region of Switzerland with the greatest earthquake risk. In the past there were several strong quakes here. That is why special rules for earthquake-proof building apply in the Valais.
wichtigste: The Visp earthquake of 25 July 1855 was one of the strongest quakes in Switzerland.
On 25 January 1946 the ground shook in the area of the Wildhorn and the Rawil.
An aftershock on 30 May 1946 set off a rockfall on the Rawilhorn.
The Valais Rhône Valley lies in the highest earthquake zone, Z3b.
Soft loose sediments in the valley strengthen the earthquake waves.
Since 2018 all building projects in the Valais have had to be planned to withstand earthquakes.

abschnitte.text: The strength of an earthquake is described in two ways. The **magnitude** is a single value for the whole quake and measures the energy released. The **intensity**, by contrast, describes the **effect at a particular place**. It is graded according to observed damage and how strongly people feel the quake. Intensity decreases with distance from the focus of the quake.

On **25 July 1855** the **Visp earthquake** took place. It had an estimated magnitude of around 6.4 and is regarded as one of the strongest quakes in Switzerland in recent centuries. Numerous buildings and churches were damaged, and rockfalls broke loose in the Mattertal. On **25 January 1946** the epicentre lay in the area of the **Wildhorn and the Rawil** north of Sion. A strong aftershock on 30 May 1946 set off a **rockfall** on the Rawilhorn.

abschnitte.titel: Why the Rhône Valley is especially at risk
abschnitte.text: According to the standard **SIA 261**, the Valais Rhône Valley is assigned to earthquake zone **Z3b**. That is the highest earthquake zone in Switzerland, with possible shaking of intensity VIII to IX. The ground beneath adds to this: the valley is filled with thick, soft **loose sediments**. These deposits amplify the ground movement, a little like jelly wobbling. The damage there can be greater than on solid rock.

For places such as **Sion** or **Brig-Visp**, so-called **spectral microzonation maps** were drawn up. They show how strongly the **local ground** changes the earthquake waves at a place. In this way it is known where the ground shakes especially strongly. Buildings can then be planned and calculated accordingly.

Since **1 January 2018** the Valais building law has required all building projects to comply with the earthquake standards **SIA 260 ff.** The canton checks this in the **building permit procedure**. Because of the dense development in the Rhône Valley, the canton expects damage of **4.5 to 10 billion francs** in a quake of magnitude 6 near Sion. That is why precaution is regarded as especially important.

gewusst: An earthquake can set off further natural hazards: in 1946 an aftershock brought a mass of rock crashing down on the Rawilhorn.
Soft ground can strengthen earthquake waves, which is why it often shakes more in the valley than on rock.

teile.einleitung: A **catchment area** is the whole area from which water flows into a particular river. Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe, and its water flows into different seas. Here you can find out where the rain goes in the different parts of the country.
wichtigste: A catchment area includes all the land that drains into a river.
The boundary between two catchment areas is called a watershed.
About two thirds of Switzerland drains via the Rhine into the North Sea.
Geneva belongs to the catchment area of the Rhône.
From the Val Poschiavo the water flows to the Po, from the Val Müstair to the Adige.
In the “Water Castle” near Brugg, water from about 40 per cent of Switzerland collects.

abschnitte.text: Every raindrop flows downhill into a stream and finally into a river. All the areas whose water reaches the same river form its **catchment area**. The boundary between two catchment areas is called a **watershed**. It mostly runs along **mountain ridges** and **passes**. On one side the water flows into one river, on the other side into another.

abschnitte.titel: The Rhine and the North Sea
abschnitte.text: About **two thirds** of the area of Switzerland drains via the **Rhine**. For the **Aare**, **Reuss** and **Limmat** also belong to its area. Even **Lake Neuchâtel** in the west belongs to it: it drains via the Zihl into Lake Biel and from there with the Aare to the Rhine. In this way this water finally reaches the **North Sea**.

Near **Brugg** in the canton of Aargau the **Aare**, **Reuss** and **Limmat** flow together close to one another. Here the water from about **40 per cent** of the Swiss land area collects. That is why this place is called the **Water Castle of Switzerland**. Shortly afterwards the Aare flows into the Rhine.

The water from the Valais and from **Geneva** belongs to the area of the **Rhône**, which flows into the Mediterranean. The **Arve** from France also belongs there. From Ticino and the **Val Poschiavo** the water flows to the **Po**. The Poschiavino flows into the Adda and this into the Po, which enters the Adriatic. From the **Val Müstair** the **Rom** flows to South Tyrol into the **Adige**. The **Inn** from the Engadine flows via the Danube into the Black Sea.

gewusst: Although Lake Neuchâtel lies in the far west of Switzerland, its water ends up in the North Sea.
Water from Switzerland reaches four seas: the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Adriatic and the Black Sea.

teile.einleitung: The **Doubs** is a river that rises in France, forms part of the border with Switzerland for a stretch and makes a great loop through the canton of Jura. It is known for deep, wooded valleys and the waterfall **Saut du Doubs**.
wichtigste: The Doubs rises near Mouthe in the French Jura.
From Les Brenets it forms the border between Switzerland and France.
The Saut du Doubs is a waterfall about 27 metres high.
The loop called Clos du Doubs lies entirely on Swiss soil in the canton of Jura.
The Doubs flows into the Saône, and its water reaches the Mediterranean.
Source and mouth are only about 90 kilometres apart.

abschnitte.text: The Doubs rises near **Mouthe** in the **French Jura** from a **karst spring**. Karst is limestone rock in which the water flows underground and comes out again at springs. The river is around **450 kilometres** long but makes huge detours. As the crow flies, source and mouth are only about **90 kilometres** apart.

At the Neuchâtel village of **Les Brenets** the Doubs begins to form the **border** between Switzerland and France. There lies the **Lac des Brenets**. At the end of the lake the river plunges about **27 metres** down at the **Saut du Doubs**. You can reach the waterfall on foot or by **boat** across the lake.

abschnitte.titel: The loop in the canton of Jura
abschnitte.text: Further downstream the Doubs flows right into Switzerland. The great river loop is called the **Clos du Doubs**. It is about 29 kilometres long and lies entirely on Swiss soil in the **canton of Jura**. On it lies the pretty little town of **Saint-Ursanne**. After that the river turns back towards France.

abschnitte.titel: All the way to the Mediterranean
abschnitte.text: At **Verdun-sur-le-Doubs** in France the Doubs flows into the **Saône**. The Saône flows into the **Rhône** and this into the **Mediterranean**. In this way part of the Jura belongs to the catchment area of the Rhône. Most other rivers of northern Switzerland, by contrast, flow via the Rhine into the North Sea.

gewusst: The Doubs is around 450 kilometres long, although source and mouth are only about 90 kilometres apart.
You can travel to the Saut du Doubs by boat across the Lac des Brenets.

teile.einleitung: The Franches-Montagnes, in German called the Freiberge, are a high plateau in the Jura. With their wide pastures, single fir trees and horses they are among the special landscapes of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Franches-Montagnes lie mostly in the canton of Jura.
In German they are called the Freiberge.
The main town is Saignelégier.
The high plateau lies at about 1,000 m above sea level.
Typical are wooded pastures, pastures with single fir trees.
In the north and north-west the Doubs forms the boundary of the Franches-Montagnes.

abschnitte.titel: A high plateau in the Jura
abschnitte.text: The **Franches-Montagnes** lie in the south-west of the **canton of Jura**, and a small part belongs to the canton of Bern. In German they are called the **Freiberge**, which means “free mountains”. In the Middle Ages settlers who cleared the land received special **freedoms**. The main town is **Saignelégier**.

Typical of the Franches-Montagnes are the **wooded pastures**, called **Wytweiden** in German. These are pastures with trees on which cows and horses graze between single **fir trees**. Forest and pasture merge into one another. This landscape came about through the work of the farmers over centuries. Wooded pastures cover about a third of the Franches-Montagnes.

The high plateau lies at about **1,000 m above sea level**. The winters are long and cold. The ground consists of **limestone**, which has turned to karst. That means rainwater seeps into cracks and drains away underground. That is why there are hardly any streams on the plateau. In the north the **Doubs** has dug a deep valley.

The Franches-Montagnes are the home of the **Franches-Montagnes horse**, called the **Freiberger** in German, the only native breed of horse in Switzerland. In Saignelégier a large **horse market** takes place every year in August, the Marché-Concours. A well-known nature area is the **Étang de la Gruère**. This bog lake was dammed in the 17th century for a mill and is protected today.

gewusst: The Franches-Montagnes horse is a calm, strong horse that used to be used mainly in farming and in the army.
In winter the Franches-Montagnes are a popular area for cross-country skiing.

teile.einleitung: A hazard map shows where natural hazards such as floods, avalanches, landslides or rockfall can threaten people and buildings. In Switzerland it helps to build safely.
wichtigste: Hazard maps show dangers with the colours red, blue, yellow and yellow and white.
Red means considerable, blue moderate and yellow low danger.
The level results from intensity and probability of occurrence.
Events that occur about every 30, 100 and 300 years are studied.
The cantons draw up the hazard maps, based on the Forest Act and the Hydraulic Engineering Act of 1991.
They become binding through the land-use planning of the municipalities.

abschnitte.titel: What is a hazard map for?
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are many **natural hazards**: floods, avalanches, landslides and rockfall. A **hazard map** shows which areas are threatened and how strongly. In this way it can be decided where building is allowed and where protection is needed. The **cantons** are responsible for the maps, and the Confederation supports them with expertise and money.

**Red** means considerable danger, and there you may not build anything new as a rule. **Blue** is the regulation area with moderate danger: building is allowed with conditions, for example with reinforced walls. **Yellow** is the information area with low danger. **Yellow and white hatching** shows a residual danger from very rare events. That is important for hospitals, for example.

For the classification two quantities are combined: the **intensity**, that is, how strong an event is, and the **probability of occurrence**, that is, how often it happens. Events that occur about every **30, 100 and 300 years** are studied. Frequent strong events give red, rare weak ones yellow. For avalanches an area counts as a red zone from a pressure of **30 kN/m²**.

The **Forest Act** and the **Hydraulic Engineering Act** of **1991** oblige the cantons to record endangered areas. The Forest Act concerns avalanches, landslides and falling processes, the Hydraulic Engineering Act floods. The maps only become binding for landowners when the municipalities take them over into **land-use planning**, that is, into the zoning plan and building regulations.

gewusst: An avalanche pressure of 30 kN/m² corresponds to about 3 tonnes per square metre and can destroy normal buildings.
Hazard maps are revised when new protective structures are built or new events occur.

teile.einleitung: Zurich Airport in Kloten is the largest airport in Switzerland. From here millions of people fly all over the world every year.
wichtigste: Zurich Airport has the code ZRH.
It has three runways, the longest being runway 16/34 at about 3,700 m.
In 2025 about 33 million passengers used the airport.
The airline Swiss has its most important base in Zurich.
Flights are normally allowed from 6 am to 11 pm.
Since 1980 the airport has had a railway station of its own.

abschnitte.text: Every airport has a code of three letters, the **IATA code**. Zurich has **ZRH**, Geneva has GVA. In 2025 Zurich Airport counted about **33 million passengers**, more than ever before. The airline **Swiss** has its **hub** here: many travellers only change planes in Zurich.

The airport has **three runways**. The longest is **runway 16/34** at about 3,700 m, then come 14/32 at about 3,300 m and 10/28 at about 2,500 m. The numbers stand for the compass direction of the runway. Because some runways cross, running the airport is complicated.

Since **1980** there has been a **railway station** under the terminal. Long-distance trains and suburban trains run directly to the airport. To **Dock E** runs the **Skymetro**, a small train that glides on a cushion of air. Right next to the airport stands **The Circle**, a large building complex with hotels, offices and shops, opened in 2020.

Aircraft make noise. That is why take-offs and landings are normally allowed only from **6 am to 11 pm**. To make up for delays, flying is still allowed until 11.30 pm. The airport lies close to the border. **Germany** forbids approaches over southern Germany at certain times, in the evening, at night and in the early morning.

gewusst: The Skymetro floats on a cushion of air instead of rolling on wheels.
From Zurich Airport you are in the main station in about ten minutes by train.

teile.einleitung: The Glacier Express is a famous panoramic train through the Swiss Alps. It links Zermatt with St Moritz and takes its time so that passengers can enjoy the views.
wichtigste: The Glacier Express runs between Zermatt and St Moritz.
It is known as the “slowest express train in the world”.
The whole journey takes about 8 hours.
The highest point is the Oberalp Pass.
The train has existed since 1930.
It is run by the Rhaetian Railway and the Matterhorn Gotthard Railway.

abschnitte.text: The **Glacier Express** runs between **Zermatt** and **St Moritz**. The journey takes about **8 hours**. That is why people call it, with a wink, the **“slowest express train in the world”**. The train has existed since **1930**. It is run by the **Rhaetian Railway** and the **Matterhorn Gotthard Railway**.

The carriages have large **panoramic windows** that reach up into the roof. This means you can also see the high peaks above the train. On the way, the train crosses around **291 bridges** and goes through many tunnels. A well-known structure is the Landwasser Viaduct near Filisur in the Grisons.

The highest point of the line is the **Oberalp Pass** at around 2,033 m above sea level. In the past the train also went over the Furka. Since **1982** it has passed through the **Furka Base Tunnel** beneath the pass. This means the train can run all year round.

The line has **metre gauge**: the rails are one metre apart. That is narrower than on most railways on flat ground. Narrow-gauge railways can take tighter bends, which is handy in the mountains. On steep sections a **rack rail** between the rails helps.

gewusst: Part of the line belongs to the UNESCO World Heritage Site “Rhaetian Railway in the Albula/Bernina Landscapes”.
On the Glacier Express, food is served directly at your seat.

teile.einleitung: The city of St Gallen wanted to draw heat from deep inside the Earth to warm its homes. The geothermal project was planned on a large scale, but had to be abandoned.
wichtigste: In 2010, around 83 per cent of the voters in the city of St Gallen approved the project.
The framework credit was 159 million francs.
The drilling site was in the Sittertobel.
The heat was mainly meant to flow into the city's district heating network.
In July 2013 the drilling triggered an earthquake of magnitude around 3.5.
Because too little hot water flowed, the power plant was not built.

abschnitte.text: On 28 November 2010, the voters of the **city of St Gallen** approved a **framework credit** of **159 million francs** with around **83 per cent**. This was to pay for drilling, a power plant and the expansion of the **district heating network**. The city wanted to replace heating oil and natural gas with local, renewable heat.

The project was **hydrothermal**: the aim was to bring up hot water from a water-bearing rock layer, an **aquifer**, at a depth of around 4,000 metres. The cooled water was to flow back down through a second borehole. Drilling took place from the **Sittertobel**, in the west of the city. At depth they measured around **140 to 145 °C**, as expected.

In July 2013, **natural gas** unexpectedly flowed into the borehole at a depth of around 4,450 metres. To stabilise it, heavy drilling fluid was pumped in. On 20 July 2013 the ground shook with a **magnitude of around 3.5**. The quake was clearly felt in the region, but caused only slight damage.

In tests, only about 6 litres of hot water flowed per second instead of the roughly 50 litres needed. Running the plant economically was therefore not possible. The city gave up the power plant.
